title: Query syntax versus method syntax
hook: from row in csv where ... select is not SQL. The compiler rewrites it to Where and Select on whatever sequence you gave it.

sections.heading: Three parts of a query, two spellings
sections.prose: Microsoft’s introduction is still the interview scaffold: obtain a source, create a query, execute the query. Creating the query does not hit the source. Query syntax leads with from so the range variable is in scope for where and select — the opposite order of SQL. Method syntax is a chain of extension members. The C# spec defines the translation; you should not claim one is faster. Readability decides. Count, ToList, and First have no from-clause spelling; you append them as methods either way.

snippets.label: Same CSV filter, both spellings
snippets.explanation: let becomes a transparent identifier, implemented as an extra Select. Execution still waits for foreach or a materializing operator.

sections.heading: Mixing and translation
sections.prose: You can write (from x in xs where p(x) select x).ToList(). Nested from becomes SelectMany. group … by … becomes GroupBy. join … on … equals … becomes Join; into makes GroupJoin. If the source is IQueryable, those methods are Queryable’s overloads that take expression trees. The syntax on the page looks identical. That identical look is the trap the IQueryable topic unpacks.

snippets.label: Query syntax plus a method that has no keyword
snippets.explanation: Count is immediate. The where/select plan runs once inside Count. There is no query-syntax count clause.

interviewTakeaways: Query syntax translates to method calls; no magic SQL.
from is first so the range variable is in scope — unlike SQL SELECT-first.
Some operators are method-only: Count, Any, ToList, ElementAt.
Identical lambdas become Func on IEnumerable and Expression on IQueryable.
commonPitfalls: Assuming query syntax talks to a database because it looks like SQL.
Writing SQL-style SELECT ... FROM in C# and expecting it to compile.
Forgetting that let allocates an extra projection.

jsTsCorrelations.note: rows.filter(...).map(...) is method syntax. JS has no query-expression compiler. Each Array method usually returns a new array immediately — eager — unlike LINQ’s deferred Where.
